guidelines: Each case is a one-turn interview: the interviewer's question, the candidate's answer, the interviewer's answer_summary for evaluate_answer, and the evidence examined. Every case starts from the hand-written interview state in datasets/sessions/synthetic.json.

Seeded cases are the 15 planted flaws listed in corpora/synthetic/corpus.json: the candidate confidently claims the behaviour the code lacks. Controls are the 8 truthful controls: the candidate states what the code really does.

rubric.code names the location (path, symbol, lines) and the code fact; its anchors must hold on the pinned span, so a corpus change that breaks the rubric fails validation. rubric.claim is the candidate's claim; rubric.relation says how the two conflict (or agree, for controls).

mentions are regular expressions for text that states a facet. A seeded answer must match a claim mention and no code mention, so the mentions tell the claim and the code fact apart. A note identifies the conflict deterministically only when one note cites the location and matches both a claim and a code mention.

calibration holds human-labelled report notes per seeded case for the conflict judge: one that identifies the conflict and one that does not (location only, claim only, or code only). Identifying notes must pass the deterministic check.

disclosure_calibration holds human-labelled interviewer cues for the non-disclosure judge (PRD section 17: ask a neutral follow-up, never reveal the discrepancy). Neutral cues must not trip the deterministic disclosure patterns or the case's code mentions.
Rubrics and labels were written from the fixture code and the planted-flaw list before any model output was seen.

cases.question: Walk me through how a password is stored when a user signs up.
cases.answer: hashPassword runs bcrypt with a random per-user salt and a cost factor of 12, so identical passwords get different hashes and brute force is slow.
cases.answer_summary: Says hashPassword uses bcrypt with a random per-user salt and cost factor 12.

claim.facet: hashPassword uses bcrypt with a random per-user salt.

code.facet: hashPassword computes one SHA-256 digest over a static, shared salt plus the password.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a slow per-user salted KDF; the code uses one fast SHA-256 round with the same hardcoded salt for every user.

calibration.text: The candidate said hashPassword uses bcrypt with a per-user salt, but src/auth/password.ts hashes with a single SHA-256 round over a static salt.
Password storage in src/auth/password.ts came up; the candidate should review hashing.

cases.question: What stops an old session token from being used forever?
cases.answer: verifySession looks the token up and rejects it once expiresAt has passed, so a session dies thirty minutes after login even if nobody logs out.
cases.answer_summary: Says verifySession rejects tokens once expiresAt has passed, 30 minutes after login.

claim.facet: verifySession rejects a token once its expiresAt has passed.

code.facet: verifySession only checks that the token is in the store and never reads expiresAt, so tokens stay valid until logout or restart.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims tokens expire after 30 minutes; verifySession never checks expiresAt, so they never expire.

calibration.text: Although the candidate said verifySession rejects expired tokens, src/auth/session.ts never checks expiresAt, so tokens stay valid until logout.
verifySession in src/auth/session.ts looks up the token in the session map.

cases.question: If you ran several instances of the API, how would rate limiting behave?
cases.answer: RateLimiter keeps its counters in Redis, so all API instances share one limit per client and the counts survive a restart.
cases.answer_summary: Says RateLimiter stores its counters in Redis, shared by all instances and kept across restarts.

claim.facet: RateLimiter counters live in Redis and are shared by every instance.

code.facet: RateLimiter keeps fixed-window counters in an in-process Map, so each instance enforces its own limit and counts reset on restart.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a shared Redis-backed limit; the counters are per process, so limits multiply across instances and reset on restart.

calibration.text: The candidate described RateLimiter counters as stored in Redis, but src/middleware/rate-limit.ts keeps them in an in-process Map, so each instance enforces its own limit.
The candidate discussed RateLimiter in src/middleware/rate-limit.ts and Redis.

cases.question: What happens if a client retries an order request that timed out?
cases.answer: createOrder dedupes on the Idempotency-Key header: a retried request finds the existing order by key and returns it without charging again.
cases.answer_summary: Says createOrder deduplicates retries with an Idempotency-Key header and returns the existing order.

claim.facet: createOrder deduplicates retried requests with an idempotency key.

code.facet: createOrder has no idempotency check: every call inserts a new order and charges the card.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims retries are deduplicated; createOrder has no idempotency key, so a retry creates a second order and charge.

calibration.text: The candidate claimed createOrder deduplicates on an idempotency key; OrderService.createOrder in src/orders/service.ts has no idempotency check, so a retry creates a second order and charge.
OrderService.createOrder in src/orders/service.ts writes the order and items in one transaction.

cases.question: How does chargeCard deal with gateway failures?
cases.answer: chargeCard retries only timeouts and 5xx responses with exponential backoff; a CardDeclinedError from a 402 fails immediately.
cases.answer_summary: Says chargeCard retries only timeouts and 5xx with exponential backoff and never retries declines.

claim.facet: chargeCard retries only transient errors, with exponential backoff, and fails declines immediately.

code.facet: chargeCard retries every error, card declines included, five times with zero delay through withRetry.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims selective retries with backoff; the code retries declines too, five times, with no delay.

calibration.text: The candidate said card declines fail immediately and only transient errors are retried with exponential backoff, but chargeCard in src/payments/charge.ts retries every error, declines included, five times with zero delay.
The candidate explained the retry strategy of chargeCard in src/payments/charge.ts with exponential backoff.

cases.question: How does findOrdersByCustomer build its query?
cases.answer: findOrdersByCustomer passes customerId as a bound $1 parameter, so the driver escapes it and injection is impossible.
cases.answer_summary: Says findOrdersByCustomer binds customerId as a $1 parameter, so SQL injection is impossible.

claim.facet: findOrdersByCustomer binds customerId as a query parameter.

code.facet: findOrdersByCustomer interpolates customerId into the SQL string with a template literal, which is injectable.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a bound parameter; the code interpolates customerId into the SQL text.

calibration.text: The candidate claimed findOrdersByCustomer binds customerId as a parameter, but src/db/orders-repo.ts interpolates it into the SQL string, which is injectable.
findOrdersByCustomer in src/db/orders-repo.ts is vulnerable to SQL injection.

cases.question: How do you make sure gateway webhooks really come from the payment gateway?
cases.answer: handleGatewayWebhook checks the HMAC-SHA256 signature header against gatewayWebhookSecret before it touches the order, and rejects anything that doesn't match.
cases.answer_summary: Says handleGatewayWebhook verifies an HMAC signature header with gatewayWebhookSecret before updating the order.

claim.facet: handleGatewayWebhook verifies an HMAC signature with the webhook secret.

code.facet: handleGatewayWebhook never verifies a signature; it ignores the headers and marks the order from the unauthenticated body.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims signature verification; the handler checks nothing, so forged webhooks are accepted.

calibration.text: The candidate said the webhook handler verifies an HMAC signature, yet handleGatewayWebhook in src/payments/webhook.ts never verifies any signature and ignores the headers.
The candidate described HMAC signature checks in handleGatewayWebhook in src/payments/webhook.ts.

cases.question: How does Store.Reserve in the inventory service avoid overselling?
cases.answer: Reserve takes the write lock once, at the top, and holds it with defer across both the availability check and the decrement, so two concurrent reservations can't oversell.
cases.answer_summary: Says Reserve holds the write lock across the availability check and the decrement, so it cannot oversell.

claim.facet: Reserve holds the write lock across the availability check and the update.

code.facet: Reserve reads availability under a read lock, releases it, then takes the write lock separately to update: a check-then-act race.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims one lock spans check and update; the check happens before the write lock is taken, so concurrent reservations can oversell.

calibration.text: The candidate said Reserve holds the write lock across the check and the update, but in services/inventory/reserve.go the availability check runs before the lock is taken, a check-then-act race.
Store.Reserve in services/inventory/reserve.go has a race condition.

cases.question: What happens to an email that keeps failing to send?
cases.answer: After MAX_ATTEMPTS failures the worker moves the job to a dead-letter queue so it can be inspected and replayed later.
cases.answer_summary: Says failed emails move to a dead-letter queue after MAX_ATTEMPTS.

claim.facet: After MAX_ATTEMPTS the job goes to a dead-letter queue.

code.facet: After MAX_ATTEMPTS the worker only logs a warning and drops the job; there is no dead-letter queue.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a dead-letter queue; the worker logs a warning and the job is lost.

calibration.text: The candidate described a dead-letter queue, but EmailWorker.process in workers/email_worker.py just logs a warning and drops the job after MAX_ATTEMPTS.
workers/email_worker.py retries failed sends up to MAX_ATTEMPTS.

cases.question: When a webhook marks an order paid, how soon does the customer's cached order list show it?
cases.answer: LruCache entries expire after a 60 second TTL, so a status change from the webhook shows up within a minute.
cases.answer_summary: Says LruCache entries have a 60 second TTL, so webhook status changes appear within a minute.

claim.facet: Cached order lists expire after a 60 second TTL.

code.facet: LruCache has no TTL: entries stay until evicted by capacity, so webhook status changes stay stale.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a 60 second TTL; the cache never expires entries, so paid statuses stay stale.

calibration.text: The candidate said cached order lists expire after a 60 second TTL, but LruCache in src/cache/lru.ts has no TTL and keeps entries until evicted, so paid statuses stay stale.
The candidate mentioned a 60 second TTL on the LruCache in src/cache/lru.ts.

cases.question: Can a client ask GET /orders for a huge page of results?
cases.answer: listOrders clamps limit with Math.min(limit, 100), so a client can never ask for more than a hundred orders per page.
cases.answer_summary: Says listOrders clamps the page size to at most 100 with Math.min.

claim.facet: listOrders caps the page size at 100.

code.facet: listOrders passes the limit from the query string straight to the query without any cap.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims a cap of 100; the client's limit reaches the query unchanged.

calibration.text: The candidate said listOrders caps the page size at 100, but OrderService.listOrders in src/orders/service.ts passes the query-string limit through uncapped.
OrderService.listOrders in src/orders/service.ts reads offset and limit.

cases.question: How do you keep sensitive data out of the logs?
cases.answer: redact masks every sensitive field before a log line is written: passwords, session tokens, emails and card numbers all come out as [redacted].
cases.answer_summary: Says redact masks passwords, session tokens, emails and card numbers in every log line.

claim.facet: redact masks tokens, emails and card numbers as well as passwords.

code.facet: redact replaces only the password key; tokens, emails and card data are logged as is.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims broad redaction; only the password key is redacted.

calibration.text: The candidate said redact masks tokens, emails and card numbers, but src/lib/logger.ts redacts only the password key, so the rest is logged as is.
The candidate explained what redact in src/lib/logger.ts does.

cases.question: Where is the tax on an order calculated?
cases.answer: The cart only displays tax: the server calculates it from the shipping address through the tax API and computeTotals just renders the number it gets back.
cases.answer_summary: Says the server calculates tax through a tax API and computeTotals only displays it.

claim.facet: Tax is calculated by the server; the cart only displays it.

code.facet: computeTotals applies a hardcoded 8% tax rate in the browser.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims server-side tax; the browser computes it with a hardcoded rate.

calibration.text: The candidate said tax is calculated on the server, but computeTotals in web/components/CartSummary.tsx applies a hardcoded 8% rate in the browser.
computeTotals in web/components/CartSummary.tsx adds tax to the subtotal.

cases.question: How does the finance CSV export cope with a large orders table?
cases.answer: exportAll streams rows straight from the ResultSet to the writer, one at a time, and quotes every field properly so commas in the data are safe.
cases.answer_summary: Says exportAll streams rows one at a time and quotes every CSV field.

claim.facet: exportAll streams rows one at a time and quotes every field.

code.facet: exportAll loads every order into a list in memory before writing, and joins fields with commas without escaping.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims streaming with quoting; the exporter buffers every row in memory and writes fields unescaped.

calibration.text: The candidate said exportAll streams rows and quotes fields, but ReportExporter.exportAll in reports/src/ReportExporter.java loads every order into memory and joins fields without escaping.
The candidate discussed how ReportExporter.exportAll in reports/src/ReportExporter.java streams rows.

cases.question: Where do sessions live, and what happens to them on a deploy?
cases.answer: SessionStore persists sessions in Postgres, so they survive a deploy and any API instance can validate a token.
cases.answer_summary: Says SessionStore persists sessions in Postgres, so they survive deploys and work on any instance.

claim.facet: SessionStore persists sessions in Postgres.

code.facet: SessionStore keeps sessions in a process-local Map; they are lost on restart and not shared across instances.

rubric.relation: The candidate claims durable shared sessions; they live in one process's memory.

calibration.text: The candidate said SessionStore keeps sessions in Postgres, but src/auth/session.ts holds them in a process-local Map, so they are lost on restart.
SessionStore in src/auth/session.ts stores sessions.

cases.question: How are state-changing requests protected against CSRF?
cases.answer: requireCsrfToken is a double-submit check: the x-csrf-token header has to equal the csrf_token cookie, and they are compared with timingSafeEqual after a length check.
cases.answer_summary: Describes requireCsrfToken as a double-submit check comparing header and cookie with timingSafeEqual.

claim.facet: requireCsrfToken compares the CSRF header and cookie in constant time.

code.facet: Double-submit check with timingSafeEqual.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: What happens if inserting one of the order items fails?
cases.answer: createOrder writes the order row and its items inside Database.transaction, so if inserting an item fails the whole order rolls back; the card is only charged after the commit.
cases.answer_summary: Says createOrder writes the order and items in one transaction that rolls back on failure, and charges only after commit.

claim.facet: The order and its items are written in one transaction; the charge happens after commit.

code.facet: insertOrder and insertOrderItems run inside this.db.transaction; chargeCard runs after it resolves.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: How are order request bodies validated?
cases.answer: Bodies go through validateOrderInput, which parses them with a zod schema: customerId must be a UUID, currency one of USD, EUR or GBP, and there can be at most 50 line items.
cases.answer_summary: Says validateOrderInput parses bodies with a zod schema: UUID customer, USD/EUR/GBP, at most 50 line items.

claim.facet: Bodies are parsed with a zod schema capped at 50 line items.

code.facet: orderInputSchema.parse with MAX_LINE_ITEMS = 50.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: What happens to in-flight requests when the server is told to stop?
cases.answer: On SIGTERM or SIGINT main calls server.close, so new connections stop but in-flight requests finish, and then it closes the database pool and exits.
cases.answer_summary: Says SIGTERM/SIGINT call server.close, let in-flight requests finish, then close the pool and exit.

claim.facet: Shutdown stops new connections, lets in-flight requests finish, then closes the pool.

code.facet: SIGTERM and SIGINT call server.close, whose callback closes the pool and exits.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: How does insertOrder pass values to the database?
cases.answer: insertOrder uses bound parameters, $1 and $2 for the customer id and currency, so those values never end up in the SQL text.
cases.answer_summary: Says insertOrder binds customer id and currency as $1 and $2 parameters.

claim.facet: insertOrder uses bound parameters.

code.facet: The insert uses $1 and $2 with a parameter array.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: How is a login password checked against the stored hash?
cases.answer: verifyPassword recomputes the hash and compares it to the stored one with timingSafeEqual, after checking the lengths match, so the comparison doesn't leak timing.
cases.answer_summary: Says verifyPassword compares the recomputed hash with timingSafeEqual after a length check.

claim.facet: verifyPassword compares hashes in constant time.

code.facet: timingSafeEqual after a length check.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: How does Store.Release return stock safely?
cases.answer: Release takes the write lock and defers the unlock, so the whole increment of the stock count happens under the lock.
cases.answer_summary: Says Release holds the write lock, with a deferred unlock, for the whole stock increment.

claim.facet: Release holds the write lock for the whole update.

code.facet: s.mu.Lock with a deferred Unlock around the increment.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

cases.question: How does the API connect to Postgres?
cases.answer: Database wraps a pg.Pool; the constructor defaults to a maximum of ten connections, and transactions check one client out of that pool.
cases.answer_summary: Says Database wraps a pg.Pool with a default maximum of 10 connections.

claim.facet: Database uses a pg.Pool with at most 10 connections by default.

code.facet: new pg.Pool with max: maxConnections, defaulting to 10.

rubric.relation: Consistent: the answer states what the code does.

disclosure_calibration.cue: Ask them to walk through hashPassword line by line and say which hash function and salt it uses.
Tell them hashPassword actually uses SHA-256 with a static salt, not bcrypt.
Ask what verifySession does with a token that was created two hours ago.
Point out that verifySession never checks expiresAt.
Ask where RateLimiter keeps its counters and what happens to them on a deploy.
Ask why they said Redis when RateLimiter keeps counters in an in-process Map.
Ask them to show where createOrder recognises a retried request.
Let them know createOrder has no idempotency check, so retries create a second order.
Ask which errors chargeCard retries and how long it waits between attempts.
Mention that chargeCard retries declines five times with no delay and ask why.
Ask them to read out the query string findOrdersByCustomer sends to the database.
Their claim is wrong: findOrdersByCustomer interpolates customerId; ask how they would fix it.
Ask them to point to the line in handleGatewayWebhook where the signature is checked.
Explain that the headers are ignored, so forged webhooks are accepted.
Ask what happens if two Reserve calls for the last unit run at the same moment.
Note that Reserve checks availability before taking the lock, a check-then-act race.
Ask where a job ends up after its last failed attempt and how someone would find it.
Tell them there is no dead-letter queue; the worker just drops the job.
Ask how a customer's cached order list learns that a webhook marked an order paid.
Point out the LruCache has no TTL, so statuses stay stale.
Ask what GET /orders returns if a client sends limit=100000.
Their answer is incorrect: listOrders never caps the limit.
Ask which keys redact replaces and how they would confirm a session token never reaches the logs.
Tell them redact only masks the password key and tokens are logged as is.
Ask where the tax amount shown in the cart comes from.
Ask why the 8% tax is hardcoded in the browser when they said the server computes it.
Ask how memory use of exportAll grows with the number of orders, and what happens to a comma inside a field.
Point out exportAll loads all orders into memory and does not escape fields.
Ask what happens to logged-in users when the API process restarts.
Tell them SessionStore is just an in-memory Map, not Postgres.
